title: Anatomy of a press release editors actually publish
hook: Is your press release being read by editors… or opened and closed? 👀

sources.name: Cision
sources.title: 2025 State of the Media Report (press release, 7 May 2025)

slides.title: anatomy of a press release editors *actually publish*
the headline is *news*, not a slogan
slides.body: Subject + action + impact. Aim for 10–14 words with a number or a place name.
slides.ex:
✕ "Innovation Without Limits"
✓ "Penang Logistics Start-up Opens 5 Northern Hubs, Cuts Delivery Times to One Day"

slides.title: the lead answers 5W1H in *two sentences*
slides.body: Editors decide in seconds. If paragraph one doesn't say **what, who, when, where and why now**, that is where reading stops.

slides.title: one quote with an *actual opinion*
slides.body: A quote is not the place for "we are thrilled". Give a point of view, a number or a plan a reporter can lift.
slides.ex:
✕ "We are thrilled to announce this milestone."
✓ "Next-day delivery shouldn't be a Klang Valley privilege. The northern region is just the start."

slides.label: of journalists call press releases the *most useful resource* from PR teams
slides.body: Press releases aren't dead. Releases a newsroom can't use straight away are.

slides.title: a body that is *ready to use*
items: Inverted pyramid: the most important fact first
Data with a comparison (up from what, to what?)
A media contact who actually picks up

slides.title: the boilerplate: *3 sentences* everyone underrates
slides.body: Who you are, since when, how big, where, and your official link. Write it once, refresh it every quarter. Journalists copy it as is.

slides.title: check these 3 *before you hit send*
items: Headline: subject, action and a number?
Quote: an opinion or a data point?

captions_meta.hook: Is your press release being read by editors… or opened and closed? 👀
lines: Editors decide in seconds. Here's what the ones that get published have in common:
03 One quote with an opinion, not "we're thrilled"
04 Body: inverted pyramid, data, photos, contact
72% of journalists still call press releases the most useful thing PR teams send (Cision, 2025).
captions_meta.li_hook:
72% of journalists say press releases are the most useful resource PR teams provide.
The format isn't the problem. Most releases just can't be used as they are.
li_body: Cision's 2025 State of the Media report (3,000+ journalists, 19 countries) is often quoted as proof that "releases still work". The part that gets skipped: journalists use the releases that save them work, not the ones that create more.
For Malaysian teams, the releases that end up published tend to share the same anatomy:
li_points: The headline is news: subject + action + impact, 10–14 words, ideally with a number or a location.
The lead answers 5W1H in two sentences. If it doesn't, the editor stops there.
The quote carries a point of view or data, not a line about being thrilled.
The body uses an inverted pyramid with comparative numbers, high-res photos and a contact who responds.
A three-sentence boilerplate refreshed every quarter, because journalists copy it verbatim.

captions_meta.fb: Before you hit "send", check your press release against this anatomy. Five parts decide whether an editor runs it 👇
